521.quote_or_event: “They alone are my friends, who travel along with me; and in that place, where the accounts are called for, they appear standing with me.”
521.explanation: In a Soohee hymn Guru Nanak defines a true friend (sajan) as one who stays at your side to the very end, even at the final reckoning when everything else has fallen away.
521.tie_back: The Kural says only kin keep faith with a man who has lost everything; Guru Nanak likewise measures a real bond by whether it still holds when nothing else remains.
521.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
521._accuracy_note: Strong fit on loyalty that outlasts loss, but Gurbani speaks of friends at the divine reckoning rather than of blood kin standing by a ruined man.

522.quote_or_event: “You are my Relative, and You are my Brother. You are my Protector everywhere; why should I feel any fear or anxiety?”
522.explanation: Guru Arjan addresses God as the kinsman and brother whose care never fails, and finds in that bond freedom from all fear.
522.tie_back: The Kural prizes kin whose love never fails; for Guru Arjan the one kinsman whose love truly never fails is God, and the gift is fearlessness rather than ever-growing wealth.
522.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 103, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
522._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the image of unfailing kinship is shared, but Gurbani transfers it to God and says nothing about kin as a source of prosperity.

523.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
523.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the state reached in the company of the holy, in which the heart mixes freely with all and no one remains an outsider.
523.tie_back: The Kural warns that a life without heart-to-heart mingling with one's people is like a tank without banks; Guru Arjan's open fellowship with everyone is the very opposite of that isolation.
523.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
523._accuracy_note: Partial: both value close fellowship, but Gurbani's is universal rather than kin-centred and says nothing about wealth draining away without it.

524.quote_or_event: Every Sikh gurdwara has its langar, a communal refectory, where all who come sit together in one straight line, none placed ahead to claim higher status or behind to mark inferiority; the distinctive Sikh langar arose as a protest against caste.
524.explanation: The community's resources are spent on a common kitchen that gathers everyone, kin and stranger alike, around a shared meal.
524.tie_back: The Kural says the real fruit of wealth is to live surrounded by one's people; the langar turns shared resources into a gathered community, though Sikhism widens that circle to everyone.
524.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Sikhism: Sikh practice” by W. H. McLeod (paraphrase)
524._accuracy_note: Reasonable: wealth used to draw people together is common to both, but the langar is open to all and is a community institution rather than one man's kin around him.

525.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
525.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak names sweetness and humility as the very core of every good quality.
525.tie_back: The Kural says kin gather in circle after circle round one who gives freely and speaks kindly; Guru Nanak places that sweetness at the heart of virtue.
525.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
525._accuracy_note: Partial: sweetness of manner matches the Kural's kind speech, but the line does not mention giving or tie these virtues to keeping kin.

526.quote_or_event: “Fareed, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger.”
526.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, tells the listener to repay wrong with good and never let anger settle in the mind.
526.tie_back: The Kural says no one has more people at his side than the generous man who does not nurse anger; Farid joins the same two things, doing good and refusing to harbour anger.
526.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
526._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on goodness without anger, though Farid's concern is the soul's purity rather than keeping kin loyal.

527.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
527.explanation: This salok is a scriptural root of kirat karni and vand chhakna: earn by honest work and share what you earn.
527.tie_back: The Kural praises the crow that does not hide its food but calls its kin to eat with it; Guru Nanak likewise makes sharing what one has the mark of the right path.
527.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
527._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the ethic of sharing; Gurbani extends sharing to all rather than one's own flock and promises the Path rather than prosperity.

528.quote_or_event: Guru Nanak passed over his own two sons and appointed his devoted disciple Lahina, renamed Angad, as his successor, because Lahina's conduct persuaded him that he was the more suitable choice.
528.explanation: Nanak judged by proven worth rather than by family claim when choosing who would lead the community.
528.tie_back: The Kural tells the ruler to give each person the regard their merit deserves rather than the same to all; Guru Nanak's choice of a successor by merit rather than birth is a Sikh instance of weighing people by worth.
528.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Sikhism: Guru Angad” by W. H. McLeod (paraphrase)
528._accuracy_note: Partial: recognising merit fits, but Sikhism also insists on equal treatment (as in the langar line) and rejects rank by caste, so the Kural's graded regard is only partly shared.

529.quote_or_event: During the siege of Anandpur forty Sikhs signed a disclaimer (bedava) renouncing Guru Gobind Singh and went home; shamed by Mai Bhag Kaur (Mai Bhago), they returned to fight beside him at Khidrana in 1705, and the Guru, finding their dying leader Maha Singh, forgave them and tore up the disclaimer. The place was renamed Muktsar, the Pool of Liberation.
529.explanation: Those who had broken away came back of their own accord, and the Guru received them as his own again.
529.tie_back: The Kural says kin who left over some grievance return by themselves once the cause of the rift is gone; the Forty Liberated Ones returned and were fully restored to their Guru.
529.source: Wikipedia, “Battle of Muktsar” (Forty Liberated Ones), paraphrase of traditional accounts
529._accuracy_note: Reasonable: return and reconciliation fit well, but the fault lay with the deserters rather than the leader, and Wikipedia is used here as a last resort for a well-known traditional account.

530.quote_or_event: “But one who feels good only when good is done for him, and feels bad when things go badly - do not call him a lover. He trades only for his own account.”
530.explanation: Guru Angad distinguishes true love from a bond kept by calculation, in which a person stays only while things go his way.
530.tie_back: The Kural tells the ruler to meet the need of the kinsman who left without cause and came back for his own purpose, and then to weigh him carefully; Guru Angad names exactly that kind of attachment: love that trades on its own account.
530.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
530._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Guru Angad is describing self-interested love for God, not a king's caution toward a returning kinsman.
